description: Sea-green, webbed with gold where it broke and broke again. It holds armour together, and gold has a way of turning up.
lore: Gold is the one thing this country never gets wrong. It arrives in the same shape whoever brings it, which is how it came to be money without anyone deciding it should be, and it is why finding gold inside a hard piece stopped several conversations the first time one of these was prised out. The mend is not set into the stone the way a jewel is set into a ring. It goes all the way through. It has been filed at, heated and worked over by people who knew their trade, and it will not come out of the sea-green and the sea-green will not come off it. The other thing everyone notices, and it is the thing that stays with you, is that it is not cold. Gold in the hand is always cold. This gold is exactly as warm as the stone around it.

Handlers grade these by the seams, and the argument about how is not settled. The long break runs the whole length and is the one everybody agrees about; it is the smaller ones that get counted, the branches off it, the hairlines that stop halfway, the mend that plainly crosses an older mend. One school holds that the count is a tally of how many seasons the animal worked its ground. Another holds that a stone is not a calendar and the count means whatever the light is doing. What is not in dispute is what the counting implies, which is that this thing broke and held, and broke and held, and went out to do the same work the following night. You do not get that from meeting one. Meeting one is a single bite and then the encounter is over.

Armourers make no claim that it stops a blow. What they claim, and what the people wearing it repeat, is that a plate with one of these in it comes apart later than it should and often does not come apart at all: it takes the hit, it opens, and it holds. A stone that is mostly mend teaches a mend. Whichever account of the gold you prefer, and there are two and neither has won, both of them are accounts of a broken thing that carried on. The rest is harder to describe and everyone carrying one describes it anyway. Gold starts turning up. A coin in the grass you would have walked over, a thread of it in a rock face you had already looked at twice. It may be that the stone finds gold. It is at least as likely that you have begun looking at the world the way that animal looked at it, taking an interest in the few things that refuse to go, and that the stone is only lending you the habit it was pressed out of.
